The file pwt_trade_world.csv has the same columns for every country in PWT 11.0 (185 economies, 1990 to 2023), plus real GDP (rgdpna, millions of 2021 US dollars) and population (pop, millions), which we use after Fig. 4. Its rows for the nine textbook countries are identical to those of pwt_trade.csv. PWT 10.01 is kept only for the nine countries, to check the textbook.

pwt_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_trade_world.csv")
pwt_world["trade_balance"] = trade_balance_share(pwt_world.csh_c, pwt_world.csh_i, pwt_world.csh_g)
print(f"{pwt_world.country.nunique()} economies, {pwt_world.year.min()}-{pwt_world.year.max()}")
185 economies, 1990-2023

The second bar of the textbook’s figure shows each country’s trade balance as a share of U.S. GDP, so the bars of different countries can be added up and compared with the U.S. deficit: we multiply the share of own GDP by the country’s GDP and divide by U.S. GDP.

You can add any country to the figure. Two small tools keep the textbook’s countries first and say which chosen countries have no data (PWT 10.01 has only the nine textbook countries).

Python note. .isin(list) is True for the rows whose value is in the list. .melt(id_vars="country") turns the two measure columns into rows, one row per country and measure, the long shape that px.bar needs. With color="Measure" and barmode="group", the bars of the two measures stand side by side. A function can return two results at once, order, missing, and the caller unpacks them into two names.

FIG3 = ["U.S.", "Japan", "China", "France", "Germany"]


def book_order(countries, book, available):
    """The chosen countries with data, the textbook's first and in its order, and the chosen ones without data."""
    order, missing = [], []
    for name in list(book) + sorted(countries):
        if name in countries and name not in order and name not in missing:
            if name in available:
                order.append(name)
            else:
                missing.append(name)
    return order, missing


def world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing):
    """The title of Fig. 3: the U.S. deficit and the largest surplus in percent of U.S. GDP."""
    if missing:
        return f"{year}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])
    if len(bars) == 0:
        return "Choose at least one country"
    text = f"{year} ({vintage}): "
    if "U.S." in bars.index:
        text += f"U.S. deficit {-bars.loc['U.S.', 'Share of own GDP']:.1f}% of GDP; "
    top = bars["Share of U.S. GDP"].idxmax()
    value = round(bars.loc[top, "Share of U.S. GDP"], 2) + 0.0     # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
    if value > 0:
        return text + f"largest surplus {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"
    return text + f"smallest deficit {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"
def world_balance_chart(year=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG3):
    """Fig. 19.3: the trade balance as a share of own GDP and of U.S. GDP, in one year."""
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    year = min(year, source[source.vintage == vintage].year.max())     # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    rows = source[(source.year == year) & (source.vintage == vintage)].set_index("country")
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG3, rows.index)
    one = rows.loc[order]
    bars = pd.DataFrame({"Share of own GDP": one.trade_balance,
                         "Share of U.S. GDP": share_of_us_gdp(one.trade_balance, one.cgdpo, rows.loc["U.S.", "cgdpo"])})
    long = bars.reset_index().melt(id_vars="country", var_name="Measure", value_name="Percent")
    fig = px.bar(long, x="country", y="Percent", color="Measure", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_map={"Share of own GDP": BLUE, "Share of U.S. GDP": GREEN},
                 labels={"country": "", "Percent": "Percent"}, title=world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    book = fit_range(long.Percent, [-9, 12.5])           # the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=book, tickvals=[-8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", title=""))
    return fig

         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(pwt_world.country.unique()), value=FIG3, rows=8,
                                  description="countries", style=WIDE));

Sources. Data: Groningen Growth and Development Centre, Penn World Table 11.0 (doi:10.34894/FABVLR) and Penn World Table 10.01, the textbook’s version (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, American Economic Review); variables csh_c, csh_i, csh_g (shares of GDP) and cgdpo (GDP at current PPPs). Prepared files: data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv and data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The United States has a deficit in every year, and France in every year since 2006. China and Germany run surpluses in every year, and Japan in 19 of the 24 years, as in the textbook.
  • Measured in U.S. GDP (green bars), China’s surplus has been the largest since 2005; before that Japan’s or Germany’s was. Germany’s surplus is large relative to its own economy, but Germany is much smaller than the United States, so its green bar is short.
  • In PWT 11.0 China’s economy at PPP has been larger than the U.S. economy since 2017, so China’s green bar is now taller than its blue bar. Choose PWT 10.01 and 2017 to see the textbook’s figure.

Key numbers: which year did the textbook plot?

The textbook’s figure is titled 2019, and the text says that “the U.S. trade deficit that year was about 4 percent of GDP”. The values below are read off the textbook’s bars.

book = pd.DataFrame({"Share of own GDP": [-4.0, 1.8, 3.0, -2.9, 7.0],

The 2017 values of PWT 10.01 reproduce the textbook’s bars within 0.05 points; the 2019 values do not (Germany 5.3, not 7.0; China 2.1, not 3.0). So the textbook’s bars are 2017 data under a 2019 title, probably left over from an earlier edition. And a newer version of the same table changes the numbers again: in PWT 11.0, Japan’s 2019 surplus is almost zero. Always check which year, and which version of a dataset, a figure really shows.

for vintage, year in [("PWT 10.01", 2017), ("PWT 11.0", 2023)]:
    one = pwt[(pwt.year == year) & (pwt.vintage == vintage)].set_index("country").loc[FIG3]
    in_us_gdp = share_of_us_gdp(one.trade_balance, one.cgdpo, one.loc["U.S.", "cgdpo"])

          f"together {in_us_gdp.drop('U.S.').sum():.2f}%")

The four other countries’ balances together are about as large as the whole U.S. deficit. China alone covers most of it.

The whole world on a map

The bars show a few countries. A map shows all 185 economies of PWT 11.0 at once, colored by their trade balance: blue for surpluses, red for deficits. Press the play button, or drag the year slider below the map.

Python note. px.choropleth colors countries on a map. locations="iso3" tells it where each row belongs, using three-letter country codes, animation_frame="year" makes one frame per year, and range_color fixes the color scale, so that the colors mean the same in every year. Balances beyond ±20 percent get the darkest color.

deficit_count = {}
for year in [1990, 2023]:
    one_year = pwt_world[pwt_world.year == year]
    deficit_count[year] = f"{(one_year.trade_balance < 0).sum()} of {len(one_year)}"
fig = px.choropleth(pwt_world, locations="iso3", color="trade_balance", hover_name="country",
                    animation_frame="year", range_color=[-20, 20], color_continuous_scale="RdBu",
                    labels={"trade_balance": "Trade balance (% of GDP)", "year": "Year"},
                    title=f"Most economies run trade deficits: {deficit_count[1990]} in 1990, "
                          f"{deficit_count[2023]} in 2023")
fig.update_layout(coloraxis_colorbar=dict(title="% of GDP"), margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=60, b=0))
fig.show()

Sources. Data: Groningen Growth and Development Centre, Penn World Table 11.0 (doi:10.34894/FABVLR) (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, American Economic Review); variables csh_c, csh_i and csh_g. Prepared file: data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv (see the data notes). Map: inspired by Fig. 19.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Deficits (red) are far more common than surpluses (blue): about two in three economies run a deficit. The world as a whole cannot run a deficit, so the surpluses of a few large economies (China, Germany, the Netherlands, the oil exporters) must offset many deficits. In the PWT data they do not offset them exactly: measured in U.S. GDP, the balances of all 185 economies add up to +3.9 percent in 2023, a reminder that trade statistics have errors.
  • Hover over a small island economy: some PWT balances are extreme, beyond −60 percent of GDP, because their consumption and investment shares are very large and poorly measured. The color scale stops at ±20 percent so that these few values do not wash out the rest of the map.

Your turn. With PWT 11.0, in which year since 2000 was the U.S. deficit largest as a share of its GDP? Was China’s surplus, in percent of U.S. GDP, also large that year? Then add Ireland and Saudi Arabia to the figure and choose 2022: which of the two had the larger surplus in percent of U.S. GDP, and was it larger than Germany’s?

Keep the U.S. rows of one version, us_pwt = pwt[(pwt.country == "U.S.") & (pwt.vintage == "PWT 11.0")], and look for the smallest value with .set_index("year").trade_balance.idxmin(). Then move the slider to that year.

# Your turn: try it here

Trade and growth around the world

Should fast-growing countries borrow from abroad to invest? Here we check whether the fastest growers really run trade deficits.

Fig. 4: The trade balance in rapidly growing countries

Goal. Test whether fast-growing countries borrow from abroad, as consumption smoothing predicts.

A country that expects to be much richer tomorrow should borrow today, like a student who expects a high income later: it should run trade deficits. The textbook checks this for five fast-growing economies. Each bar is the simple average of the yearly trade balance over a window of years. We first make a table with one row per year and one column per country, so that period_average gives one average per country.

Python note. .pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance") turns a long table into a wide one: years as rows, countries as columns. [FIG4] then keeps the columns in the textbook’s order. With text_auto=".1f", px.bar writes each bar’s value, with one decimal, on the bar.

FIG4 = ["China", "India", "Singapore", "Ireland", "S. Korea"]
fast = pwt[pwt.country.isin(FIG4)]


def fast_growers_chart(start=2000, end=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG4):
    """Fig. 19.4: the average trade balance (% of own GDP) of fast-growing (or any chosen) economies."""
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    wide = source[source.vintage == vintage].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance")
    end = min(end, wide.index.max())                         # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG4, wide.columns)
    avg = period_average(wide[order], start, end)
    bars = avg.rename("average").reset_index()
    title = f"{start}–{end} ({vintage}): {(avg > 0).sum()} of {len(avg)} economies ran trade surpluses on average"
    if missing:
        title = f"{start}–{end}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])
    fig = px.bar(bars, x="country", y="average", text_auto=".1f", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN], labels={"country": "", "average": "Percent of own GDP"},
                 title=title)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    book = fit_range(avg.dropna(), [-5, 30])                 # the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=book, tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30])
    return fig
interact(fast_growers_chart,
         start=IntSlider(value=2000, min=1990, max=2005, step=1, description="first year", style=WIDE),
         end=IntSlider(value=2023, min=2010, max=2023, step=1, description="last year", style=WIDE),
         vintage=ToggleButtons(options=["PWT 11.0", "PWT 10.01"], value="PWT 11.0", description="data"),
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(pwt_world.country.unique()), value=FIG4, rows=8,
                                  description="countries", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 4 with a precomputed slider for the last year (first year 2000, PWT 11.0)
slider_figure(fast_growers_chart, "end", [2010, 2015, 2017, 2019, 2023], start=2023, label="last year")

Sources. Data: Groningen Growth and Development Centre, Penn World Table 11.0 (doi:10.34894/FABVLR) and Penn World Table 10.01, the textbook’s version (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, American Economic Review); variables csh_c, csh_i and csh_g. Prepared files: data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv and data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • With one exception, India, these fast-growing economies run trade surpluses, not deficits. They lend to the rest of the world instead of borrowing from it.
  • This is the opposite of what consumption smoothing (the permanent-income idea of Chapter 16) predicts. The textbook suggests that the causality may run the other way: countries that push their firms to export may grow faster.
  • Singapore’s and Ireland’s averages are very sensitive to the window. Move the first year back to 1990: Singapore’s average falls from 19.3 to 10.6 percent. The next subsection shows why.

Look at your data: an average can hide big swings

annual = fast[fast.vintage == "PWT 11.0"]
low, high = annual.loc[annual.trade_balance.idxmin()], annual.loc[annual.trade_balance.idxmax()]
fig = px.line(annual, x="year", y="trade_balance", color="country", hover_name="country",
              color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GRAY, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8"],
              labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of own GDP", "country": "Country"},
              title=f"Yearly trade balances swing: {low.country} {low.trade_balance:.1f}% in {low.year}, "
                    f"{high.country} {high.trade_balance:.1f}% in {high.year}")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
fig.update_yaxes(range=[-40, 60], tickvals=[-20, 0, 20, 40, 60])
fig.show()

Sources. Data: Groningen Growth and Development Centre, Penn World Table 11.0 (doi:10.34894/FABVLR) (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, American Economic Review); variables csh_c, csh_i and csh_g. Prepared file: data/ch19/pwt_trade.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Two series behave strangely. Singapore’s balance jumps from −33 percent of GDP in 1993 to +15 percent in 1998. Singapore is a trading hub: in the Penn World Table its exports and its imports were each about two to three times its GDP in the mid-1990s, so its trade balance is a small difference between two huge numbers, and a small error in either one moves it a lot. Ireland’s balance swings from 32 percent of GDP in 2018 to 7 percent in 2019 and 50 percent in 2022: large multinational firms book much of their production and profits in Ireland, which moves its GDP and trade statistics far more than Irish living standards. Neither country’s data are “wrong”, but a single average hides all this, and it changes a lot with the choice of years. That is why the figure lets you choose the window.

Key numbers: which window did the textbook average?

The textbook’s title says 2000–2019 and its text says “from 1990 to 2019”. The values below are read off its bars.

book4 = pd.Series([2.9, -0.4, 16.1, 22.8, 3.5], index=FIG4)
wide10 = fast[fast.vintage == "PWT 10.01"].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance")
windows = pd.DataFrame({"Textbook": book4})
for start, end in [(2000, 2017), (2000, 2019), (1990, 2019)]:
    windows[f"PWT 10.01, {start}–{end}"] = period_average(wide10, start, end)
windows.round(2)
Textbook PWT 10.01, 2000–2017 PWT 10.01, 2000–2019 PWT 10.01, 1990–2019
China 2.9 2.91 2.83 2.16
India -0.4 -0.36 -0.25 -0.59
Singapore 16.1 16.13 16.89 7.63
Ireland 22.8 22.75 22.61 17.70
S. Korea 3.5 3.51 3.73 2.82

Only the window 2000–2017 reproduces the bars, within 0.05 points: like Fig. 3, the figure uses the data up to 2017. The text’s window, 1990–2019, would give Singapore 7.6 instead of 16.1. The finding itself does not depend on the window: India is the only deficit country in every column.

Beyond the textbook’s five: do fast-growing economies borrow?

The textbook picked five fast-growing economies. A fairer test uses every economy: does faster growth go with smaller trade balances (borrowing), as consumption smoothing predicts? We measure growth of real GDP per person, rgdpna / pop, from 2000 to 2023, and the average trade balance over the same years.

Python note. growth_rate applies the growth formula of Chapter 3 to every column of the wide table at once. np.log is the natural logarithm. pd.DataFrame({...}).dropna() builds the table of two columns and drops the economies that miss either one.

def growth_rate(y, start, end):
    """Average annual growth rate in percent: 100 ln(y_end / y_start) / (end - start)."""
    return 100 * np.log(y.loc[end] / y.loc[start]) / (end - start)


pwt_world["gdp_per_person"] = pwt_world.rgdpna / pwt_world["pop"]
income = pwt_world.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdp_per_person")
balance = pwt_world.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance")
growers = pd.DataFrame({"growth": growth_rate(income, 2000, 2023),
                        "trade_balance": period_average(balance, 2000, 2023)}).dropna().reset_index()
growers.sort_values("trade_balance").head(7).round(1)
country growth trade_balance
19 Bermuda 0.7 -2232.4
167 Turks and Caicos Islands -0.8 -189.2
3 Anguilla 0.7 -83.8
112 Montserrat 2.9 -76.8
151 St. Kitts and Nevis 1.7 -44.2
14 Barbados 0.7 -40.1
95 Lesotho 1.7 -38.9

Look at your data. A few small island economies have average “balances” of −40 to −2,200 percent of GDP (Bermuda). These are not real trade deficits: PWT’s consumption and investment shares are badly measured for such tiny, finance-heavy economies. We set aside the economies beyond ±40 percent and say so.

Python note. np.where(test, a, b) takes a where the test is True and b elsewhere: here a label for the textbook’s five and an empty text for the others. trendline="ols" with trendline_scope="overall" fits one straight line through all the points, whatever their color.

odd = growers[growers.trade_balance.abs() > 40]
print(f"Set aside: {', '.join(odd.country)}")
growers = growers[growers.trade_balance.abs() <= 40].copy()
growers["group"] = growers.country.isin(FIG4).map({True: "Textbook's five", False: "Other economies"})
growers["label"] = np.where(growers.country.isin(FIG4), growers.country, "")
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(growers.growth, growers.trade_balance, 1)
fig = px.scatter(growers, x="growth", y="trade_balance", color="group", text="label", hover_name="country",
                 trendline="ols", trendline_scope="overall",
                 color_discrete_map={"Textbook's five": GREEN, "Other economies": GRAY},
                 labels={"growth": "Growth of GDP per person, 2000–2023 (% a year)",
                         "trade_balance": "Average trade balance (% of GDP)", "group": ""},
                 title=f"{len(growers)} economies: 1 point faster growth, {slope:+.1f} points of trade balance")
fig.update_traces(textposition="top center", marker_size=9)
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), selector=dict(mode="lines"))
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
fig.show()
print(f"Correlation: {growers.growth.corr(growers.trade_balance):.2f}")
Set aside: Anguilla, Barbados, Bermuda, Montserrat, St. Kitts and Nevis, Turks and Caicos Islands
Correlation: -0.22

Sources. Data: Groningen Growth and Development Centre, Penn World Table 11.0 (doi:10.34894/FABVLR) (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, American Economic Review); variables csh_c, csh_i, csh_g, rgdpna (real GDP) and pop (population). Prepared file: data/ch19/pwt_trade_world.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.4 and the discussion in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Across all economies the fitted line slopes down: economies that grew faster ran smaller trade balances on average, as consumption smoothing predicts. But the link is weak (a correlation of about −0.2), and many fast growers sit on both sides of zero.
  • The textbook’s five are not typical. Of the 28 economies that grew faster than 4 percent a year, only 5 ran surpluses on average; many of the others (Ethiopia, Cambodia, Armenia) borrowed from abroad or received aid.
  • So the textbook’s puzzle is mostly a puzzle about East Asian exporters and Ireland. A data science lesson: a conclusion drawn from five hand-picked countries can change when you look at all of them.

Your turn. The first year slider stops at 2005. Compute the averages for the window 2010–2023 (PWT 11.0) in code. How many of the five economies run a surplus on average then, and which one changes sign? Then find the fastest-growing economy in growers: did it run a surplus or a deficit?

Make the wide table of PWT 11.0 first: wide11 = fast[fast.vintage == "PWT 11.0"].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance"). Then period_average(wide11, 2010, 2023) gives all five averages at once. For the second question, sort the table growers with .sort_values("growth") and look at its last rows.

# Your turn: try it here

The twin deficits

The identity \(NX = S - I\) links the trade balance to saving. This section compares the U.S. budget deficit, investment and the trade deficit over time.

Fig. 5: U.S. investment, budget deficit, and trade deficit

Goal. See the twin deficits: large budget deficits that come with large trade deficits.

Equation (4) says \(NX = S - I\): a country that saves less than it invests must borrow the difference abroad. When the government runs a larger budget deficit, government saving \(T - G\) falls, and so does domestic saving \(S\). Either investment falls too, or foreigners fill the gap and the trade deficit grows. The file has the three series of the textbook’s figure, as percent of GDP.

twin = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig19-5.csv").set_index("year")
twin.head()
investment_pct_gdp budget_deficit_pct_gdp trade_deficit_pct_gdp
year
1960 15.944 -0.029 -0.775
1961 15.401 0.842 -0.874
1962 16.058 0.889 -0.679
1963 16.203 0.339 -0.775
1964 16.385 1.007 -1.010

The trade deficit is minus the trade balance, so \(NX = -\)(trade deficit). With our function domestic_saving we add a fourth line, domestic saving \(S = I + NX\). The gap between saving and investment is then exactly the trade deficit.

Python note. rename(columns={...}) gives the columns readable names, which then appear in the legend.

named = twin.rename(columns={"investment_pct_gdp": "Investment", "budget_deficit_pct_gdp": "Budget deficit",
                             "trade_deficit_pct_gdp": "Trade deficit"})
named["Domestic saving, S = I + NX"] = domestic_saving(named.Investment, -named["Trade deficit"])
gap = net_capital_outflow(named["Domestic saving, S = I + NX"], named.Investment)
print(f"S - I equals minus the trade deficit in every year: {((gap + named['Trade deficit']).abs() < 1e-9).all()}")
named.loc[[1979, 1986, 2006, 2025]].round(2)
S - I equals minus the trade deficit in every year: True
Investment Budget deficit Trade deficit Domestic saving, S = I + NX
year
1979 20.54 1.80 0.86 19.68
1986 18.54 4.72 2.88 15.66
2006 19.55 1.61 5.69 13.86
2025 18.01 5.76 2.98 15.02

The menu chooses an episode with a rising budget deficit. The title reports how much each line changed between the first and the last year of the episode.

Python note. named.loc[end] - named.loc[start] subtracts two rows, column by column. Dropdown is a menu, and list(EPISODES) lists the keys of the dictionary, the names of the episodes.

EPISODES = {"1980s: 1979 to 1986": (1979, 1986), "2000s: 2000 to 2006": (2000, 2006),
            "Great Recession: 2007 to 2010": (2007, 2010), "Covid-19: 2019 to 2021": (2019, 2021)}
LINES = ["Investment", "Budget deficit", "Trade deficit", "Domestic saving, S = I + NX"]


def twin_deficits_chart(episode="1980s: 1979 to 1986"):
    """Fig. 19.5: investment, the budget deficit and the trade deficit (% of GDP), with one episode."""
    start, end = EPISODES[episode]
    change = named.loc[end] - named.loc[start]
    fig = px.line(named.reset_index(), x="year", y=LINES, color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, BLUE, GREEN, GRAY],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP"},
                  title=f"{start}→{end}: budget deficit {change['Budget deficit']:+.1f}, trade deficit "
                        f"{change['Trade deficit']:+.1f}, investment {change['Investment']:+.1f} points")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name=LINES[3]), line_width=2, line_dash="dot")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.2, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1958, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5, 28], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25])        # room for the legend
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"),
                      legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(twin_deficits_chart, episode=Dropdown(options=list(EPISODES), value="1980s: 1979 to 1986",
                                               description="episode", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version

                                               "Great Recession: 2007 to 2010", "Covid-19: 2019 to 2021"],
              start="1980s: 1979 to 1986")

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), National Income and Product Accounts, via FRED: Gross private domestic investment (GPDIA), Federal government net saving (FGDEF), Gross domestic product, quarterly (GDP), Net exports of goods and services (A019RC1A027NBEA) and Gross domestic product (GDPA). Prepared file: data/ch19/fig19-5.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • From 1979 to 1986 the budget deficit rose by 2.9 points of GDP and the trade deficit by 2.0 points; investment fell by 2.0 points, but it stayed high by historical standards. Foreign saving paid for part of the government’s borrowing: the first episode of twin deficits.
  • From 2000 to 2006 the pattern repeats: the budget deficit rose by 3.2 points and the trade deficit by 2.0 points, while investment hardly changed (−0.3).
  • In the Great Recession the twins split: the budget deficit soared, investment collapsed, and the trade deficit fell. In the Covid-19 years the budget deficit jumped by more than 7 points, the trade deficit rose by less than 1 point, and investment barely moved. Click “Domestic saving” in the legend to hide it; the gap between it and investment is the trade deficit.

Key numbers: decades of twin deficits

Python note. named.index // 10 * 10 turns each year into its decade (1987 → 1980): // divides and drops the remainder. .groupby(...) then puts the years of each decade together, and .mean() averages them.

decades = named.groupby(named.index // 10 * 10).mean().round(2)
decades.index.name = "decade"
decades

1990 17.33 2.64 1.26 16.07
2000 17.98 2.59 4.54 13.43
2010 16.89 5.00 3.02 13.87

Compared with the 1970s, the 1980s had higher budget deficits (4.0 against 3.5 percent of GDP) and much higher trade deficits (1.75 against 0.18), with no fall in investment (18.5 against 18.0). Domestic saving has drifted down, from about 17 percent of GDP in the 1960s and 1970s to 13–15 percent since 2000, and the trade deficit has filled the gap.

Beyond the United States: twin deficits in other countries

Did large budget deficits come with large trade deficits elsewhere too? The file twin_deficits_world.csv has the three lines of Fig. 19.5 for most economies, as percent of GDP, from 1980 to 2025:

  • investment: gross capital formation (World Bank WDI NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS). It includes government investment, so it is higher than the private investment of Fig. 5;
  • budget_deficit: minus the net lending of the general government, federal plus state and local (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026, GGXCNL_NGDP; the last year or two are IMF estimates). For the United States the IMF series starts only in 2001;
  • trade_deficit: minus the WDI trade balance of Figs. 1 and 2.

The same names can hide different definitions, so we first compare the U.S. rows with the BEA data of Fig. 5.

twin_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "twin_deficits_world.csv")
us_world = twin_world[twin_world.country == "U.S."].set_index("year")
pd.DataFrame({"Investment, private (BEA)": named.Investment, "Investment, all (WDI)": us_world.investment,
              "Budget deficit, federal (BEA)": named["Budget deficit"],
              "Budget deficit, all governments (IMF)": us_world.budget_deficit,
              "Trade deficit (BEA)": named["Trade deficit"], "Trade deficit (WDI)": us_world.trade_deficit}
             ).loc[[2007, 2009, 2020, 2024]].round(1)
Investment, private (BEA) Investment, all (WDI) Budget deficit, federal (BEA) Budget deficit, all governments (IMF) Trade deficit (BEA) Trade deficit (WDI)
year
2007 18.5 22.6 1.8 2.9 5.1 5.1

The trade deficits agree within 0.1 point, but total investment is about 4 points higher than private investment, and the general-government deficit is about 1 point higher than the federal one. The figure function draws the three lines for any economy; its title reports the correlation of the two deficits, a number between −1 and +1 that is positive when they rise and fall together.

Python note. a.corr(b) is the correlation of two columns. .stack() puts all the columns of a table into one long column, so that fit_range sees every value of the three lines.

WORLD_LINES = {"investment": "Investment", "budget_deficit": "Budget deficit", "trade_deficit": "Trade deficit"}
counts = twin_world.dropna(subset=["budget_deficit", "trade_deficit"]).groupby("country").year.count()
TWIN_COUNTRIES = sorted(counts[counts >= 5].index)     # economies with both deficits in at least 5 years


def twin_deficits_world(country="U.S."):
    """Fig. 19.5 for any economy: investment, budget deficit and trade deficit, percent of GDP."""
    one = twin_world[twin_world.country == country].rename(columns=WORLD_LINES)
    both = one.dropna(subset=["Budget deficit", "Trade deficit"])
    r = round(both["Budget deficit"].corr(both["Trade deficit"]), 2) + 0.0
    fig = px.line(one, x="year", y=list(WORLD_LINES.values()), color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP"},
                  title=f"{country}, {both.year.min()}–{both.year.max()}: correlation of the budget and "
                        f"trade deficits {r:+.2f}")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1975, 2027])         # 1980 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(one[list(WORLD_LINES.values())].stack(), [-5, 28]))
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0, y=-0.15, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"),
                      legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(twin_deficits_world, country=Dropdown(options=TWIN_COUNTRIES, value="U.S.", description="economy",
                                               style=WIDE));

In the general-government data since 2001, the two U.S. deficits are negatively correlated (−0.36): the largest budget deficits came in the recessions of 2009 and 2020, when the trade deficit shrank. Twin deficits are clearer in Germany (+0.57) and Greece (+0.56), where both deficits rose together before the euro crisis and fell together after it. Over long periods the “twins” are only loosely related: what matters is what happens to private saving and investment at the same time.

# Your turn: try it here

Net foreign assets and foreign debt

Years of trade deficits add up to a debt to the rest of the world. We measure that debt for the United States and for every other economy.

Fig. 6: Net international investment position of the United States

Goal. Follow how decades of trade deficits turned the United States from a lender into a debtor.

The net international investment position (NIIP) is what U.S. residents own abroad (foreign shares, bonds, factories) minus what foreigners own in the United States, at the end of each year. When it is negative, it is the net foreign debt. Each year’s trade deficit is new borrowing, so the position should fall by about the size of the deficit. With our function accumulate, we start from the 1976 position and add the trade balance of every later year, as in the Oddtopia table. We also compare the current data with the same series as published in July 2023, which the textbook used.

niip = pd.DataFrame({
    "Current data": share_of_gdp(us.niip, us.gdp),
    "As published in July 2023 (the textbook)": share_of_gdp(us.niip_2023, us.gdp_2023),
    "1976 position + sum of later trade balances": share_of_gdp(accumulate(us.niip[1976], us.net_exports.loc[1977:]),
                                                                us.gdp)})

niip.loc[[1980, 1988, 1989, 2008, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2025]].round(1)

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), International Investment Position and National Income and Product Accounts, via FRED: U.S. net international investment position (IIPUSNETIA), Gross domestic product (GDPA) and Net exports of goods and services (A019RC1A027NBEA); the July 2023 vintages of IIPUSNETIA and GDPA via ALFRED. Prepared file: data/ch19/us_trade.csv, checked against data/ch19/fig19-6.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Until 1988 the United States was a net creditor: it owned more abroad than foreigners owned in the United States. Since 1989 it has been a net debtor, and its net foreign debt has grown to about 70 percent of GDP.
  • The dotted line adds up the trade balances since 1976. It has the same downward trend: the foreign debt is, roughly, the sum of past trade deficits. But the gap between the two lines is large in some years (37 points of GDP in 2010), because the position also changes when asset prices and the dollar move, and with the income earned on foreign assets. Until 2020 these effects kept the debt below the summed deficits; in 2021 and since 2023 it is above them.
  • The textbook’s data (dashed) show a trough of about −80 percent in 2021. BEA has since revised the series: the current data are 9 to 16 points of GDP less negative for 2020–2022, and the deepest point is now 2024.

Key numbers: the foreign debt

The textbook says that the United States was a net creditor “up until the late 1980s” and that its net foreign debt “exceeded 60 percent of GDP in 2022”.

july_2023 = niip["As published in July 2023 (the textbook)"].dropna()

print(f"Revision to the 2021 position: {(us.niip[2021] - us.niip_2023[2021]) / 1000:+.2f} trillion dollars")
change, summed = us.niip[2025] - us.niip[1976], us.net_exports.loc[1977:2025].sum()
print(f"1976 to 2025: position {change / 1000:+.1f} trillion dollars; sum of trade balances {summed / 1000:+.1f} trillion")

In the textbook’s vintage the net foreign debt was 63.5 percent of GDP in 2022, as the text says. In the current data it is 54.6 percent for 2022, because BEA has revised the position upward by 1.9 to 3.4 trillion dollars for 2020–2022. The statement still holds for the most recent years: the debt is above 60 percent of GDP in 2021 and in 2023–2025. Over the whole period, trade deficits of 18.0 trillion dollars came with a fall of 22.0 trillion in the investment position.

Beyond the United States: creditors and debtors around the world

The BEA measures only the U.S. position. For other countries, economists use the External Wealth of Nations database of Philip Lane and Gian Maria Milesi-Ferretti (Brookings, release of February 2026), which collects and completes the official investment positions of about 200 economies. The file niip_world.csv has the net position (foreign assets minus foreign liabilities, gold included) as a percent of GDP, both in US dollars, at the end of each year from 1970 to 2024. First we check its U.S. rows against the BEA data of the figure above.

When you combine sources, check that they measure the same thing at the same vintage.

def niip_world_chart(countries=("U.S.",)):
    """Fig. 19.6 for any economies: net international investment position, percent of GDP."""
    rows = niip_world[niip_world.country.isin(countries)]
    if len(rows) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Choose at least one economy"))
    last = rows.groupby("country").last()                  # each economy's latest year
    names = []
    for name in last.index[:2]:
        names.append(f"{name} {round(last.niip[name]) + 0:+d}%")
    more = f" + {len(last) - 2} more" if len(last) > 2 else ""
    fig = px.line(rows, x="year", y="niip", color="country", hover_name="country", color_discrete_map=COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "niip": "Percent of GDP"},
                  title="Latest net foreign assets, % of GDP: " + ", ".join(names) + more)
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1965, 2027])         # 1970 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(rows.niip, [-100, 30]))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(niip_world_chart,

The United States has by far the largest net foreign debt in dollars (27 trillion in this database), but not as a share of GDP: Greece’s (−132 percent) and those of several small or poor economies are larger.
