# Your turn: try it here

Concluding remarks

  • Trade has become much more important: U.S. exports and imports have risen from about 4 percent of GDP each in 1950 to 11 and 14 percent. Since 1976 imports have exceeded exports every year, and the trade deficit reached 5.7 percent of GDP in 2006.
  • The national income identity shows what a deficit means. With \(NX < 0\), a country uses more than it produces (equation 1), and it invests more than it saves, \(NX = S - I\) (equation 4). The deficit is borrowing from the rest of the world, and past deficits add up to the net foreign debt (equation 5), about 70 percent of U.S. GDP today. In present value, trade has to balance over time (equation 6), and a steady deficit leads to a stable debt ratio only if GDP grows faster than the return on the debt (equation 7).
  • Trade can make everyone better off: across time it shares risks (Oddtopia and Eventopia), and across goods it lets countries specialize by comparative advantage. In the North–South model the world price of equation (10) lies between the two autarky prices of equation (9), condition (11), and each country gains in the good it imports. Free migration follows absolute advantage and raises world output even more.
  • The data hold surprises: the textbook’s fast-growing economies run surpluses, not deficits, and the large U.S. budget deficits of the 1980s and 2000s came with large trade deficits (the twin deficits). Looking beyond the textbook’s countries changes both stories: across all economies, faster growth goes with slightly smaller trade balances, and the twin deficits are clear in some countries (Germany, Greece) but not in others.
  • The data also teach care: the textbook’s “2019” bars are 2017 data, revisions changed the recent U.S. foreign debt by up to 16 points of GDP, and two sources for the same country can differ by vintage and definition.
  • The next chapter, exchange rates and international finance, brings trade into the short-run model and asks how the exchange rate adjusts.

Practice problems

These problems let you use the chapter’s tools in three ways: conceptual problems apply the identities and the trade models to real cases, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data, and modeling problems use small calculators built on the Model overview to answer policy questions. Each problem is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it on your own first, then open the Hint, and open the Solution last. The calculators run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top of the page); on the website, each solution reports what its calculator shows.

Conceptual problems

Problem 1 (Basic): Japan’s trade deficits after Fukushima. After the Fukushima nuclear accident of 2011, Japan took all of its nuclear reactors offline for safety checks, and its power companies had to import large amounts of liquefied natural gas instead (U.S. Energy Information Administration). In the World Bank data of Fig. 2, Japan’s trade balance turned negative for five years. Its current account, however, stayed positive (IMF, World Economic Outlook, current account balance):

2011 2012 2013 2014 2015
Trade balance, % of GDP (World Bank) −0.64 −1.63 −2.38 −2.55 −0.54
Current account, % of GDP (IMF) 2.1 0.9 0.9 0.7 3.0

  1. The Model overview defines the current account as \(CA_t = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1}\). Use it to compute Japan’s net income from its foreign assets in each year, in percent of GDP.

  2. At the end of 2010, Japan’s net foreign assets were 54.7 percent of GDP (the External Wealth of Nations data of Fig. 6). What average return \(\bar{r}\) does your number for 2011 imply? Ignore the growth of GDP.

  3. By the end of 2015, Japan’s net foreign assets had risen to 61.1 percent of GDP. How can a country run trade deficits for five years and still end up a bigger creditor? Answer with equation (5).

Hint

The income from foreign assets is the gap between the current account and the trade balance. For (b), divide that income by the assets held at the start of the year. For (c), write equation (5) as \(F_t - F_{t-1} = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1}\): which flow changes the stock of assets, the trade balance or the current account?

Your answer:

Solution

(a) Solve the definition for the income term, \(\bar{r}F_{t-1} = CA_t - NX_t\). In percent of GDP:

2011 2012 2013 2014 2015
\(CA - NX\) \(2.1 + 0.64 = 2.74\) \(0.9 + 1.63 = 2.53\) \(0.9 + 2.38 = 3.28\) \(0.7 + 2.55 = 3.25\) \(3.0 + 0.54 = 3.54\)

On average Japan earned about 3.1 percent of GDP a year from abroad, more than enough to pay for its trade deficits. (The data’s current account also counts transfers such as aid and remittances, which the model leaves out, so these gaps are the income from foreign assets plus net transfers.)

(b) Divide the income by the assets at the start of the year:

\[\bar{r} \approx \frac{\bar{r}F_{2010}}{F_{2010}} = \frac{2.74}{54.7} = 0.050,\]

a return of about 5 percent a year. That is high for a safe investment. The reason is that the income is earned on gross positions, which are much larger than the net one: if what Japan owns abroad earns more than what it owes foreigners costs, the return on the net position looks high.

(c) Equation (5) says \(F_t - F_{t-1} = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} = CA_t\): net foreign assets grow by the current account, not by the trade balance. From 2011 to 2015 Japan’s trade balances add up to \(-0.64 - 1.63 - 2.38 - 2.55 - 0.54 = -7.74\) percent of a year’s GDP, but its current accounts add up to \(2.1 + 0.9 + 0.9 + 0.7 + 3.0 = 7.6\) percent, so its claims on the rest of the world kept growing. The data show a rise of \(61.1 - 54.7 = 6.4\) points; the rest of the difference comes from changes in asset prices, in the yen and in GDP. A creditor can run trade deficits for as long as they are smaller than its income from abroad. A debtor is in the opposite position: its interest payments make its current account weaker than its trade balance.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Norway’s oil fund and the spend-only-the-return rule. Norway puts its government’s oil and gas revenue into the Government Pension Fund Global, which invests abroad. A fiscal rule says that, over time, the government may spend only the fund’s expected real return, now estimated at 3 percent a year, and never its capital. At the end of 2025 the fund was worth about NOK 21,300 billion, almost four times Norway’s GDP (norskpetroleum.no, run by Norway’s Ministry of Energy and its Offshore Directorate). In our data, Norway’s net foreign assets were 358 percent of GDP at the end of 2024 (the file of Fig. 6), and its trade surplus averaged 12.2 percent of GDP from 2000 to 2024 (the file of Fig. 2).

Take a stylized Norway whose foreign assets \(F\) earn a real return of \(\bar{r} = 0.03\).

  1. Suppose that, once the oil runs out, Norway runs a trade deficit equal to the return on its assets in every year, \(NX_t = -\bar{r}F_{t-1}\). Show with equation (5) that its foreign assets then never change. What is its current account?

  2. Show that this plan satisfies the intertemporal budget constraint, equation (6), for a creditor with \(F_0 > 0\), as the horizon \(T\) goes to infinity. You may use \(\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} 1/(1+\bar{r})^t = 1/\bar{r}\).

  3. Now measure the assets relative to GDP, \(f = F/Y = 3.58\). With no growth of GDP, how large a trade deficit, in percent of GDP, does the rule allow? With real GDP growth of \(\bar{g} = 0.02\), which constant trade balance keeps \(f\) at 3.58? Why does growth lower the deficit that Norway can afford?

Hint

For (a), put the trade balance into \(F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} + NX_t\). For (b), take the constant \(\bar{r}F_0\) out of the sum. For (c), use the ratio form of equation (5) from the Model overview, \(f_t = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx_t\), set \(f_t = f_{t-1}\) and solve for \(nx\). A real return together with real growth is fine here: the ratio \(F/Y\) is the same in real and in nominal terms.

Your answer:

Solution

(a) Substitute \(NX_t = -\bar{r}F_{t-1}\) into equation (5):

\[F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} - \bar{r}F_{t-1} = F_{t-1}.\]

The assets stay at \(F_0\) forever. The current account is \(CA_t = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} = -\bar{r}F_{t-1} + \bar{r}F_{t-1} = 0\): the return pays for the extra imports, and nothing is added to or taken from the fund.

(b) With \(NX_t = -\bar{r}F_0\) in every year,

\[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = -\bar{r}F_0\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = -\bar{r}F_0 \times \frac{1}{\bar{r}} = -F_0,\]

which is equation (6). The end term of the derivation also vanishes, as it must: \(F_T/(1 + \bar{r})^T = F_0/(1 + \bar{r})^T\) goes to zero as \(T\) grows. For a creditor, equation (6) reads the other way round than for a debtor: the present value of its trade balances is negative, so it can run trade deficits forever.

(c) With no growth, \(nx = -\bar{r}f = -0.03 \times 3.58 = -0.107\): a deficit of 10.7 percent of GDP in every year. With growth, setting \(f_t = f_{t-1} = f\) gives

\[f = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f + nx \quad\Longrightarrow\quad nx = f\left(1 - \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\right) = -\frac{(\bar{r} - \bar{g})\,f}{1 + \bar{g}} = -\frac{0.01 \times 3.58}{1.02} = -0.035.\]

The rule now allows a deficit of only 3.5 percent of GDP. The return is worth \(0.03 \times 3.58/1.02 = 0.105\), or 10.5 percent of this year’s GDP, but \(0.02 \times 3.58/1.02 = 0.070\), or 7.0 points of it, must be invested abroad again, so that the fund keeps up with a growing economy. Today Norway is still far from that stage: it runs trade surpluses (12.2 percent of GDP on average since 2000), because each year it turns more oil and gas into foreign assets.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Can tariffs close the trade deficit? In April 2025 the United States put new tariffs on imports from its trading partners, by an executive order whose title names “large and persistent annual United States goods trade deficits” as the problem to fix (Executive Order 14257, Federal Register). Customs duties collected rose from 84 billion dollars in 2024 to 269 billion in 2025, or from 0.284 to 0.871 percent of GDP (BEA, Customs duties (B235RC1Q027SBEA), via FRED, annual averages of the quarterly data). The file of Fig. 5 shows the other terms of the identity, in percent of GDP:

2024 2025
Trade deficit 3.000 2.985
Federal budget deficit 6.474 5.761
Private investment 18.060 18.007

  1. Write the trade balance as in Step 5 of the saving–investment block, \(NX = (Y - T - C - I) + (T - G)\). Suppose the extra customs revenue had raised government saving \(T - G\) one for one, while private saving and investment stayed the same. By how much would the trade deficit have fallen?

  2. Now use the table. By how much did private saving minus investment, \(Y - T - C - I\), change from 2024 to 2025, according to the identity? What does that imply for private saving itself? (The budget deficit here is the federal one, so treat state and local governments as part of the private term.)

  3. Many economists argue that a tariff can lower the trade deficit only if it raises national saving or lowers investment. Explain this argument with equation (4). Give two reasons why private saving might fall when tariffs rise. Is one year of data enough to judge the policy?

Hint

For (a), the change in customs revenue, in points of GDP, goes one for one into \(NX\). For (b), solve the identity for the private term, \(Y - T - C - I = NX - (T - G) = \text{budget deficit} - \text{trade deficit}\), compute it for both years, and add back the change in investment. For (c), think about who pays a tariff and how they react, and recall that \(NX = EX - IM\): if \(S - I\) does not move, what must happen to exports when imports fall?

Your answer:

Solution

(a) Customs duties rose by \(0.871 - 0.284 = 0.587\), about 0.59 points of GDP. With the private term fixed, \(\Delta NX = \Delta(T - G) = +0.59\), so the trade deficit would have fallen from 3.00 to about 2.41 percent of GDP.

(b) The private term is the budget deficit minus the trade deficit:

\[2024:\; 6.474 - 3.000 = 3.474, \qquad 2025:\; 5.761 - 2.985 = 2.776, \qquad \text{change} = -0.698.\]

Private saving minus investment fell by about 0.70 points of GDP. Investment changed by \(18.007 - 18.060 = -0.053\), so private saving itself fell by about \(0.698 + 0.053 = 0.75\) points. In 2025 the federal government saved more (its deficit fell by 0.71 points, in part thanks to the tariffs), the private sector saved less by about the same amount, and the trade deficit hardly moved.

(c) Equation (4), \(NX = S - I\), holds whatever the tariff. Tariffs make imports dearer and may reduce them, but if national saving and investment do not change, net exports cannot change either: exports must then fall by about as much as imports. Possible channels are retaliation by other countries, a stronger dollar (Chapter 20), and imported parts that make U.S. exports dearer. Two reasons why private saving may fall:

  1. A tariff is a tax, paid by importers and, through higher prices, by households. If households keep their consumption smooth (Chapter 16), they pay it by saving less, and the rise in government saving is then offset one for one.
  2. Firms that absorb part of the tariff earn smaller profits, so business saving falls.

One year is not enough to judge. Many things change at once, and the timing of trade was distorted: in the first quarter of 2025, net exports fell to −1,215 billion dollars at an annual rate, from −944 billion in the last quarter of 2024 (BEA, Net exports of goods and services (NETEXP), via FRED), a jump that suggests importers bought ahead of the tariffs. A fair test compares several years with what saving and investment would have done without the tariffs.

Data-based problems

Problem 4 (Basic): Mexico’s opening after NAFTA. The North American Free Trade Agreement between Canada, Mexico and the United States entered into force on January 1, 1994, and its tariff cuts were phased in until 2008 (Office of the U.S. Trade Representative). Use the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, exports and imports of goods and services in percent of GDP, in the file wdi_trade.csv of Fig. 1.

  1. Compute Mexico’s openness, exports plus imports in percent of GDP, in 1993 and in 2024. By what factor did it grow?

  2. In which year was Mexico’s openness highest, and how high was it?

  3. Compute the openness of Canada and of the United States in 1993 and in 2024. Which of the three economies is the most open today?

Hint

Read the file with trade = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv") and keep one country with trade[trade.country == "Mexico"].set_index("year"). The sum of its exports and imports columns is a Series with the years as labels: .loc[[1993, 2024]] picks two years, and .idxmax() gives the year of the largest value. A loop over ["Canada", "U.S."] repeats the steps for the other two.

# Your answer here
Solution

Add the two shares, pick the years, and repeat for the neighbors:

trade = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")
mexico = trade[trade.country == "Mexico"].set_index("year")
open_mexico = mexico.exports + mexico.imports
print(open_mexico.loc[[1993, 2024]].round(1).to_dict())
print(f"Growth factor: {open_mexico[2024] / open_mexico[1993]:.1f}")
print(f"Highest: {open_mexico.max():.1f}% of GDP in {open_mexico.idxmax()}")
for name in ["Canada", "U.S."]:
    one = trade[trade.country == name].set_index("year")
    print(name, (one.exports + one.imports).loc[[1993, 2024]].round(1).to_dict())

It prints {1993: 26.2, 2024: 75.4}, a growth factor of 2.9, a peak of 88.8 percent of GDP in 2022, then Canada {1993: 58.2, 2024: 65.1} and U.S. {1993: 20.0, 2024: 25.0}.

Mexico’s openness almost tripled, and Mexico is now the most open of the three economies. Canada was already open in 1993 (it had had a free trade agreement with the United States since 1989, as the USTR page explains), and the United States remains one of the least open economies in the world. A word of caution: Mexico’s openness jumped by 14.5 points from 1994 to 1995 (from 29.15 to 43.67 percent of GDP), far faster than tariff cuts phased in over 14 years could explain. Other forces move these shares too, such as the exchange rate (Chapter 20). The data show that Mexico opened up after NAFTA; by themselves they do not tell how much of the opening NAFTA caused.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Do large economies trade less? After Fig. 1 we found the United States among the least open economies, and suggested that large economies trade less because much of their trade takes place inside their own borders. Test this for 2023 with two measures of size from Penn World Table 11.0 (file pwt_trade_world.csv): GDP at PPP (cgdpo) and population (pop). Openness is exports plus imports in percent of GDP, from the World Bank file wdi_trade.csv.

  1. Merge the 2023 rows of the two files by their country code iso3. How many economies have openness, GDP and population?

  2. Compute the correlation of the log of openness with the log of GDP, and with the log of population. Which measure of size goes with openness more closely? Why might that be?

  3. Among the 15 most populous economies, what is the median openness, and how does it compare with the median of all economies? Which of the 15 is the big exception?

Hint

a.merge(b, on="iso3") joins two tables row by row where the codes match, and .dropna(subset=[...]) drops the economies with a missing value. np.log takes the log of a whole column, and x.corr(y) gives a correlation. For (c), .sort_values("pop", ascending=False).head(15) keeps the 15 largest, and .median() gives the middle value. Write the population column as ["pop"], because .pop is also the name of a pandas method. For the “why”, think of Singapore and Ireland.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

Make openness in the World Bank file, merge, take logs, then sort by population:

trade = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")
size = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_trade_world.csv")
open_2023 = trade[trade.year == 2023].copy()
open_2023["openness"] = open_2023.exports + open_2023.imports
size_2023 = size[size.year == 2023][["iso3", "cgdpo", "pop"]]
merged = open_2023.merge(size_2023, on="iso3").dropna(subset=["openness", "cgdpo", "pop"])
print(f"{len(merged)} economies")
log_open = np.log(merged.openness)
print(f"Correlation with log GDP: {log_open.corr(np.log(merged.cgdpo)):.2f}")
print(f"Correlation with log population: {log_open.corr(np.log(merged['pop'])):.2f}")
largest = merged.sort_values("pop", ascending=False).head(15)
print(f"Median openness: {largest.openness.median():.1f}% for the 15 most populous, {merged.openness.median():.1f}% for all")
print(largest[["country", "pop", "openness"]].round(1).to_string(index=False))

It prints 156 economies, correlations of −0.18 with log GDP and −0.50 with log population, and medians of 41.3 percent for the 15 most populous economies against 79.0 percent for all of them. In the list, every large economy but one has an openness between 20.6 percent (Ethiopia) and 86.7 percent (DR Congo); the United States, at 24.9 percent, is the second lowest.

The claim holds, and it holds much more clearly for population than for GDP. GDP mixes two things: the number of people, which sets how much trade can take place inside the borders, and income per person, which has little to do with that. Several small, rich economies are trading hubs with extreme openness, such as Singapore (about 324 percent) and Ireland (about 240 percent) in 2023, and they blur the link between GDP and openness. The big exception among the 15 is Vietnam: with 100.4 million people, its openness is 165.0 percent, because its exports alone were 86.7 percent of GDP. Size makes trade less likely to be large, but it does not rule it out.

Problem 6 (Challenge): Who borrowed abroad before the euro crisis? Step 5 of the saving–investment block splits the trade balance into a private and a public part, \(NX = (Y - T - C - I) + (T - G)\). With both deficits in percent of GDP, the private part, private saving minus investment, is therefore the budget deficit minus the trade deficit. The file twin_deficits_world.csv of Fig. 5 has both deficits for most economies: the general-government budget deficit from the IMF World Economic Outlook and the trade deficit from the World Bank.

  1. Compute private saving minus investment for Greece, Portugal and Spain in 2007, just before the crisis, and in

  1. In 2007, in which country was the trade deficit the “twin” of a large budget deficit, and in which did it come mostly from private borrowing?

  2. The European Union’s rules set a reference value of 3 percent of GDP for government deficits (EUR-Lex, the excessive deficit procedure). Would a strict 3 percent rule have prevented these three trade deficits of 2007? What does your answer suggest about the numbers that policymakers should watch?

Hint

Keep the three countries and the two years with .isin([...]), combining the two tests with &, and add a column budget_deficit - trade_deficit. A negative private part means that households and firms invested more than they saved, and borrowed the difference from abroad. In this file the budget deficit includes government investment, so the private part is private saving minus private investment.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

Keep the six rows and compute the private part from the identity:

deficits = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "twin_deficits_world.csv")
keep = deficits.country.isin(["Greece", "Portugal", "Spain"]) & deficits.year.isin([2007, 2013])
euro = deficits[keep].copy()
euro["private"] = euro.budget_deficit - euro.trade_deficit      # private saving minus investment
columns = ["country", "year", "budget_deficit", "trade_deficit", "private", "investment"]
print(euro[columns].sort_values(["country", "year"]).round(1).to_string(index=False))
budget deficit trade deficit private saving minus investment investment
Greece 2007 6.8 11.0 −4.2 26.7
Greece 2013 4.1 2.3 1.8 12.1
Portugal 2007 2.9 7.6 −4.7 23.1
Portugal 2013 5.2 −1.1 6.3 14.7
Spain 2007 −1.9 5.8 −7.7 30.5
Spain 2013 7.5 −3.8 11.3 17.4

(b) Greece had twin deficits: of its trade deficit of 11.0 percent of GDP, 6.8 points came from the government and 4.2 from the private sector. Spain’s government ran a surplus of 1.9 percent of GDP, so its whole trade deficit, and more, was private borrowing (7.7 points), at a time when investment was 30.5 percent of GDP. In Portugal, private borrowing (4.7 points) was larger than the budget deficit (2.9 percent of GDP).

(c) No. Spain and Portugal respected the 3 percent reference value in 2007 and still had trade deficits of 5.8 and 7.6 percent of GDP; only Greece broke the rule. A fiscal rule watches only the second term of the identity, and the private term can be just as large. By 2013 the private sectors had swung to surpluses (Spain by \(11.3 - (-7.7) = 19.0\) points), mostly because investment collapsed, and the trade deficits had shrunk or turned into surpluses (Greece from 11.0 to 2.3 percent of GDP, Spain from a deficit of 5.8 to a surplus of 3.8). So policymakers should also watch the trade or current-account balance and private borrowing. Since the crisis, the EU also runs a Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure that aims to spot and correct harmful imbalances of this kind.

Modeling problems

Problem 7 (Basic): Paying for a hurricane. A hypothetical island economy is hit by a hurricane. To rebuild, it runs trade deficits of 5 percent of GDP for 3 years, borrowing abroad at the interest rate \(\bar{r}\), and then repays with equal trade surpluses over the next 10 years. It has no foreign assets before the storm, \(F_0 = 0\), and its GDP stays constant, so everything can be measured in percent of GDP. The calculator below applies equation (5) year by year and picks the surplus that satisfies equation (6). Answer with its sliders.

  1. If the loans are free of interest, \(\bar{r} = 0\), how large must each surplus be? Check it with equation (6).

  2. If the island borrows at a market rate of 4 percent, how large is each surplus, and how large is the debt when the rebuilding ends?

  3. A development bank offers a loan at 1 percent instead. How much smaller is each year’s surplus than at 4 percent, and how much less does the island hand over in total during the 10 years?

Hint

Read the title of the calculator for each interest rate. To check by hand: with \(\bar{r} = 0\), equation (6) says that the trade balances add up to zero. With \(\bar{r} > 0\), find the debt after the 3 years of deficits with equation (5), then pick the surplus \(S\) whose present value over 10 years equals that debt: \(S\sum_{j=1}^{10} 1/(1+\bar{r})^j = \text{debt}\).

def repayment_plan(deficit=5.0, years=3, r=0.0, repay_years=10):
    """Equations (5) and (6): trade deficits for some years, then equal surpluses that repay the debt (% of GDP)."""
    pv = 0.0
    for j in range(1, repay_years + 1):
        pv = pv + 1 / (1 + r / 100) ** j                       # present value of 1 a year (Appendix C.12)
    F, flows, assets = 0.0, [], []
    for t in range(1, years + repay_years + 1):
        nx = -deficit if t <= years else -assets[years - 1] / pv   # equation (6): the surpluses repay the debt
        F = (1 + r / 100) * F + nx                             # equation (5)
        flows.append(nx)
        assets.append(F)
    year = list(range(1, years + repay_years + 1))
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=year, y=flows, name="Trade balance, NX", marker_color=TEAL))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=year, y=assets, mode="lines+markers", name="Net foreign assets, F",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Surplus needed: {flows[-1]:.2f}% of GDP a year; peak debt {-assets[years - 1]:.1f}% of GDP",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Years after the storm", range=[0.3, 15.7]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Percent of GDP", range=[-60, 12]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.03, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))
    return fig


interact(repayment_plan,
         deficit=FloatSlider(value=5.0, min=1.0, max=10.0, step=1.0, description="deficit, % of GDP", style=WIDE),
         years=IntSlider(value=3, min=1, max=5, step=1, description="years of deficits", style=WIDE),
         r=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate r, %", style=WIDE),
         repay_years=fixed(10));

Source. A calculator built on the accounting for net foreign assets in the Model overview, equations (5) and (6), adapted from the discussion of trade across time in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here
Solution

(a) With \(\bar{r} = 0\) the island owes \(3 \times 5 = 15\) percent of GDP after the rebuilding, and equation (6) with \(F_0 = 0\) says that the trade balances must add up to zero: \(3 \times (-5) + 10\,S = 0\), so \(S = 1.5\) percent of GDP a year. The calculator’s title reads “Surplus needed: 1.50% of GDP a year; peak debt 15.0% of GDP”.

(b) With interest, the debt grows during the rebuilding. By equation (5), the debt after 3 years is

\[5\,(1.04)^2 + 5\,(1.04) + 5 = 15.61\]

percent of GDP. The surplus must have a present value equal to that debt: \(S \times 8.111 = 15.61\), where \(8.111 = \sum_{j=1}^{10} 1/1.04^j\), so \(S = 1.92\) percent of GDP a year.

(c) At 1 percent the debt is 15.15 percent of GDP and the surplus 1.60 percent a year, 0.32 points less than at 4 percent. Over 10 years the island hands over 16.00 percent of a year’s GDP instead of 19.24 percent: the cheaper loan saves it about 3.2 percent of a year’s output. The code below confirms the numbers:

for rate in [0.0, 0.04, 0.01]:
    debt, pv = 0.0, 0.0
    for k in range(3):
        debt = (1 + rate) * debt + 5                     # equation (5), for the debt
    for j in range(1, 11):
        pv = pv + 1 / (1 + rate) ** j
    surplus = debt / pv                                  # equation (6)
    print(f"r = {rate:.0%}: debt {debt:.2f}% of GDP, surplus {surplus:.2f}% a year, {10 * surplus:.2f}% in total")
print(repayment_plan(5.0, 3, 4.0, 10).layout.title.text)

It prints r = 0%: debt 15.00% of GDP, surplus 1.50% a year, 15.00% in total, then 15.61, 1.92 and 19.24 for 4 percent, 15.15, 1.60 and 16.00 for 1 percent, and the calculator’s title for 4 percent. The lesson of equation (6) is that every deficit is repaid by later surpluses; the interest rate decides how large they must be.

Problem 8 (Intermediate): How much foreign debt can the United States carry? The net foreign debt of the United States was 70.9 percent of GDP at the end of 2025 (Fig. 6), and its trade deficit has been about 3 percent of GDP for years. The calculator starts from the 2025 position and applies the ratio form of equation (5), \(f_t = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx\), for 100 years with a constant trade balance. The dashed line is the long-run ratio \(f^*\) of equation (7). Here \(\bar{g}\) is the growth rate of nominal GDP and \(\bar{r}\) the net return that foreigners earn on the debt. Answer with the sliders.

  1. With \(nx = -3\), \(\bar{g} = 4\) and \(\bar{r} = 0\) percent, does the debt ratio rise or fall from its 2025 level, and where does it settle? Which constant trade balance would hold the ratio at its 2025 level?

  2. A policy committee wants the net foreign debt never to exceed 100 percent of GDP in the long run, even if foreigners earn a net return of 2 percent on it while nominal GDP grows at 4 percent. What is the largest steady trade deficit that meets this goal? Find it roughly with the sliders, then exactly with equation (7).

  3. Suppose instead that nominal growth slows to 3 percent, the return is 2 percent, and the deficit stays at 3 percent of GDP. Where does the ratio head, and in which year does the debt pass 100 percent of GDP? Why does a small change in \(\bar{g} - \bar{r}\) matter so much?

Hint

The title shows \(f^*\) and the year in which the debt passes 100 percent of GDP. For the trade balance that holds a ratio \(f\), solve equation (7) for \(nx\): \(nx = f\,(\bar{g} - \bar{r})/(1 + \bar{g})\). For (c), compare the factor \(\frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\) in the cases, and look at the denominator of equation (7).

def debt_projection(nx=-3.0, g=4.0, r=0.0):
    """Equations (5) and (7): U.S. net foreign assets (% of GDP) if the trade balance stays at nx after 2025."""
    history = share_of_gdp(us.niip, us.gdp).dropna()                   # the BEA data of Fig. 6
    f_star = round(100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(nx / 100, g / 100, r / 100), 1) + 0.0    # equation (7)
    passed = "never above 100% of GDP" if f_star >= -100 else "above 100% of GDP only after 2125"
    ratio, path, years = history.iloc[-1] / 100, [], list(range(history.index[-1] + 1, 2126))
    for year in years:
        ratio = (1 + r / 100) / (1 + g / 100) * ratio + nx / 100       # equation (5) divided by GDP
        path.append(100 * ratio)
        if ratio < -1 and passed.endswith("2125"):
            passed = f"above 100% of GDP from {year}"
    low = -200 if min(path + [f_star]) > -190 else -700                 # a wider axis only for very large debts
    fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=history.index, y=history, mode="lines", name="BEA data", line=dict(color=GRAY, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=path, mode="lines", name="Projection", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1900, 2200], y=[f_star, f_star], mode="lines", name="Long run, f*",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_hline(y=-100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Long run: f* = {f_star:.1f}% of GDP; net foreign debt {passed}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[1970, 2130]), yaxis=dict(title="Percent of GDP", range=[low, 20]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))
    return fig


interact(debt_projection,
         nx=FloatSlider(value=-3.0, min=-6.0, max=0.0, step=0.5, description="trade balance nx, % of GDP", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=3.0, max=7.0, step=0.5, description="nominal GDP growth g, %", style=WIDE),
         r=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="return on the debt r, %", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the foreign-debt dynamics of the Model overview, equations (5) and (7), and the BEA data of Fig. 6, adapted from the discussion of foreign debt in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) The title reads \(f^* = -78.0\) percent: the debt ratio keeps rising, but slowly, from 70.9 percent toward 78.0 percent of GDP (it is still at 75.3 percent in 2050). Solving equation (7) for the trade balance that holds today’s ratio,

\[nx = f\,\frac{\bar{g} - \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = -0.709 \times \frac{0.04}{1.04} = -0.0273,\]

a deficit of about 2.7 percent of GDP keeps the net foreign debt at its 2025 level. The current deficit is only a little larger.

(b) With \(\bar{r} = 2\), the slider shows \(f^* = -104.0\) percent at \(nx = -2.0\) and \(-78.0\) percent at \(nx = -1.5\). Exactly, with \(f^* = -1\):

\[nx = -1 \times \frac{0.04 - 0.02}{1.04} = -0.0192.\]

The deficit must not exceed 1.92 percent of GDP, about two thirds of today’s deficit. A positive return on the debt adds interest to the borrowing, so the same debt ceiling allows a smaller trade deficit.

(c) Equation (7) gives \(f^* = 1.03 \times (-0.03)/(0.03 - 0.02) = -3.09\): the debt heads toward 309 percent of GDP, and the calculator shows it passing 100 percent of GDP in 2039. The long-run ratio of equation (7) has \(\bar{g} - \bar{r}\) in its denominator: with the same deficit of 3 percent, \(f^*\) is \(-156\) percent when \(\bar{g} = 4\) and \(\bar{r} = 2\), so halving the gap from 2 points to 1 point roughly doubles the debt. The factor \(\frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = 1.02/1.03 = 0.990\) is also close to one, so the ratio drifts for a very long time before it settles. If \(\bar{r}\) reached \(\bar{g}\), no stable ratio would exist, and equation (6) says that such a path cannot last. The code below confirms the numbers:

f_2025 = share_of_gdp(us.niip, us.gdp).dropna().iloc[-1] / 100
print(f"(a) f* = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, 0.04):.1f}%; the balance that holds {100 * f_2025:.1f}% "
      f"is {100 * f_2025 * 0.04 / 1.04:.2f}% of GDP")
nx_max = -1.0 * (0.04 - 0.02) / (1 + 0.04)               # equation (7) solved for nx, with f* = -1
print(f"(b) largest deficit {-100 * nx_max:.2f}% of GDP; check: f* = "
      f"{100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(nx_max, 0.04, 0.02):.1f}%")
ratio, crossing = f_2025, 0
for year in range(2026, 2126):
    ratio = 1.02 / 1.03 * ratio - 0.03                     # equation (5) divided by GDP
    if ratio < -1 and crossing == 0:
        crossing = year
print(f"(c) f* = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, 0.03, 0.02):.1f}%; the debt passes 100% of GDP in {crossing}")

It prints (a) f* = -78.0%; the balance that holds -70.9% is -2.73% of GDP, then a largest deficit of 1.92 percent (with \(f^* = -100.0\)), and \(f^* = -309.0\) percent with a crossing in 2039.

Problem 9 (Challenge): When the South grows. In the North–South model of the Model overview, let the South’s workforce \(L_s\) grow while all the other numbers stay the same. Think of a large economy with many workers joining world trade, as China did when it entered the World Trade Organization in 2001 (WTO). The calculator compares consumption per person under free trade with autarky (autarky = 100) for each good and each country; the numbers on the green bars are the amounts per person. Answer with its slider.

  1. Move \(L_s\) from 400 to 600. What happens to the world price of a computer, to apples per person in the North and to computers per person in the South?

  2. Use equations (10) and (11) to find the range of \(L_s\) for which complete specialization is the outcome, given the other numbers. What happens to the South’s gain from trade at the upper end of the range?

  3. A northern politician says that the South’s growth hurts the North; a southern politician says that a bigger South is better for southern workers. Who is right in this model? Show that the South’s total consumption of computers does not depend on \(L_s\), and explain why in words.

Hint

Equation (10) gives the world price as a function of \(L_s\). Put it into each inequality of condition (11) and solve each one for \(L_s\). For (c), multiply the South’s computers per person, \(x_s/(2p)\), by the number of southern workers, and think about what an apple buys on the world market.

def south_grows(L_s=400):
    """Equations (8) to (11): consumption per person with free trade, relative to autarky, for any size of the South."""
    closed = pd.DataFrame({"North": autarky(x_n, z_n, L_n), "South": autarky(x_s, z_s, L_s)})
    trade = free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s)
    p = trade.loc["Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"]
    labels, index, text = [], [], []
    for country in ["North", "South"]:
        for good in ["Apples", "Computers"]:
            amount = trade.loc[good + " per person", country]
            labels.append(f"{country}: {good.lower()}")
            index.append(100 * amount / closed.loc[good + " per person", country])
            text.append(f"{amount:.0f}" if good == "Apples" else f"{amount:.2f}")     # the amount per person
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=labels, y=[100, 100, 100, 100], name="Autarky", marker_color=GRAY))
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=labels, y=index, name="Free trade", marker_color=GREEN, text=text, textposition="outside"))
    note = f"between the autarky prices {x_n / z_n:.0f} and {x_s / z_s:.0f}"             # condition (11)
    if p >= x_s / z_s:
        note = "the South's gain from trade is gone"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"L_s = {L_s}: a computer costs {p:.1f} apples, {note}", barmode="group",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Consumption per person, autarky = 100", range=[0, 600]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.98, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(south_grows, L_s=IntSlider(value=400, min=200, max=800, step=50, description="southern workers L_s", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the autarky and free_trade functions of the Model overview, adapted from the apple-and-computer example in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) From \(L_s = 400\) to \(600\) the world price of a computer rises from 25.0 to 37.5 apples. Northern workers eat 300 apples instead of 200 (the bar goes from 250 to 375), and still have 8 computers. Southern workers still eat 50 apples, but have 1.33 computers instead of 2.00.

(b) By equation (10), \(p = L_s x_s/(L_n z_n) = 100\,L_s/1{,}600 = L_s/16\). Condition (11) has two parts:

\[\frac{x_s}{z_s} > p \;\Longleftrightarrow\; 50 > \frac{L_s}{16} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; L_s < \frac{L_n z_n}{z_s} = 800, \qquad p > \frac{x_n}{z_n} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \frac{L_s}{16} > 10 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; L_s > \frac{L_n x_n}{x_s} = 160.\]

So the North makes only computers and the South only apples for \(160 < L_s < 800\). As \(L_s\) approaches 800, the world price rises to 50 apples, the South’s own autarky price, and southern computers per person fall to \(x_s/(2p) = 100/100 = 1\), the autarky level: the South’s gain from trade disappears. With an even larger South, southern workers would also make computers, the price would stay at 50, and all the gains from trade would go to the North.

(c) In this model the northern politician is wrong: each northerner’s apples, \(L_s x_s/(2L_n)\), rise with \(L_s\), and computers stay at \(z_n/2 = 8\). The southern politician is wrong too: a bigger South is worse for each southern worker. Apples stay at \(x_s/2 = 50\), but computers per person, \(L_n z_n/(2L_s)\), fall as \(L_s\) grows, so each worker’s gain from trade shrinks, although nobody falls below the autarky bundle. The South’s total computers are

\[L_s \times \frac{x_s}{2p} = L_s \times \frac{L_n z_n}{2L_s} = \frac{L_n z_n}{2} = 800,\]

half of the world’s computers, whatever the size of the South. The extra southern workers make more apples, but each apple buys fewer computers on the world market, in the same proportion: the price of what the South sells falls relative to the price of what it buys. The South gets more apples, but no more computers. (In reality, as the free-migration block of the Model overview notes, switching jobs is costly, so northern workers in the industries that compete with imports can lose even when the North as a whole gains.) The code below confirms the numbers:

for workers in [400, 600, 800]:
    world_trade = free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, workers)
    p = world_trade.loc["Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"]
    north_apples = world_trade.loc["Apples per person", "North"]
    south_computers = world_trade.loc["Computers per person", "South"]
    print(f"L_s = {workers}: p = {p:.1f}, North apples {north_apples:.0f}, South computers {south_computers:.2f} "
          f"each and {workers * south_computers:.0f} in total")
print(f"Complete specialization for {L_n * x_n / x_s:.0f} < L_s < {L_n * z_n / z_s:.0f}")

It prints L_s = 400: p = 25.0, North apples 200, South computers 2.00 each and 800 in total, then 37.5, 300, 1.33 and 800 for 600 workers, 50.0, 400, 1.00 and 800 for 800 workers, and the range 160 < L_s < 800.
